extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, sponsors, applicants, and DHS adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Federal DHS rule guidance on how officers evaluate whether a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge, including how Affidavits of Support, receipt of public benefits, and statutory factors are weighed in the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will favorably consider a sufficient Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA as a positive factor in the totality of the circumstances when assessing an applicant's likelihood at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sufficient Affidavit is treated favorably alongside statutory minimum factors and receipt of public benefits, but is not outcome-determinative. DHS views the affidavit as making an applicant less likely to become a public charge, but it does not automatically overcome other adverse factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency determination and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS determines the sufficiency of a required Affidavit of Support by assessing whether the sponsor has demonstrated the means to maintain income at the required level; if an Affidavit of Support is determined to be insufficient, DHS will automatically determine the applicant inadmissible under section 212(a)(4) without consideration of the statutory minimum factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficiency is a threshold determination that occurs before the public charge totality analysis. If the affidavit is insufficient, the public charge analysis does not proceed; thus sufficiency must be established first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsor credibility not considered after sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Once DHS determines an Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA is sufficient, officers will not consider the sponsor's credibility, intent, or underlying motives in the totality of the circumstances public charge analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsor credibility/motives may be relevant in assessing sufficiency (e.g., fraud or material concealment), but reevaluating credibility in the public charge analysis would be duplicative and create unnecessary burden; therefore it is not intended to be separately considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: No presumption of admissibility from affidavit
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not treat a sufficient Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA as creating a rebuttable presumption that an applicant is not likely at any time to become a public charge, nor will DHS treat the affidavit alone as sufficient to determine admissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress created statutory minimum factors that must be considered; the affidavit is not among those mandatory factors, and DHS declines to make the affidavit outcome-determinative or to create a presumption in favor of admissibility based solely on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory consideration of statutory minimum factors
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS must consider the statutory minimum factors (age, health, family status, assets, resources, financial status, education, skills, and current or past receipt of public benefits) in every public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory factors are considered in the 'totality of the circumstances' and must be weighed in every case regardless of the presence of an Affidavit of Support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of receipt of public benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Receipt of public benefits occurs when a public benefits-granting agency provides public benefits to a noncitizen, but only where the noncitizen is listed as a beneficiary; applying for benefits or approval for future receipt generally does not constitute receipt, and benefits provided to others (including adult caregivers or household members) do not count unless the noncitizen was a named beneficiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition differs from past guidance; it is designed to avoid chilling effects on benefit use by family members and clarifies that assistance provided solely on behalf of another or by another individual will not be treated as the applicant's receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of benefits considered
rubrics_metrics.description: For public charge purposes DHS will consider public cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization at government expense; DHS generally excludes non-cash benefits (e.g., SNAP) and Home- and Community-Based Services (HCBS) from consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HHS consulted and supported excluding HCBS because they do not provide total care for basic needs and often reduce reliance on institutional care. The rule follows a standard similar to the 1999 guidance focusing on primary dependence as shown by cash assistance or long-term institutionalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of children's benefit receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: Children are not categorically exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility unless Congress expressly exempted their classification; however, benefits received by caregivers or household members will not be considered unless the child was a named beneficiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will apply the totality of circumstances to children and intends to issue guidance clarifying considerations relevant to a child's receipt of public benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active-duty service members' benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not create a special exclusion for active-duty U.S. service members and their spouses and children from consideration of public benefits in public charge determinations, because the rule already generally excludes non-cash benefits that such families commonly use and data show negligible use of TANF/SSI by active-duty noncitizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only benefits received by the applicant as a named beneficiary are considered; DHS reiterates statutory limits on exemptions and notes coordination with DOD on naturalization for service members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of amount and duration of benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The longer a noncitizen has received benefits in the past and the greater the amount of benefits, the stronger the implication that the noncitizen may be likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS recognizes variability across States/localities in program availability and amounts but nonetheless retains consideration of amount and duration as probative of likelihood to become a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term institutionalization criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term institutionalization at government expense is characterized by uninterrupted, extended periods of stay in an institution (e.g., nursing home, mental health institution) and is the only Medicaid-funded services category considered for public charge purposes; short-term rehabilitation stays or imprisonment are not considered long-term institutionalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sporadic stays with discharge are not long-term; continuous extended institutional stays—even with off-site trips—may qualify. The term was revised from prior guidance to better specify covered services and duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future approval of benefits as probative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Approval for future receipt of a public benefit does not constitute receipt, but evidence of approval for future receipt may be considered by an officer in the totality of the circumstances as probative of the probability of future receipt of public benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not treated as present receipt, such approvals can indicate a likelihood of future dependence and therefore be relevant to the predictive assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement/reimbursement not part of public charge analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The enforcement of Affidavit of Support obligations (including potential reimbursement suits by sponsored immigrants) and sponsorship enforcement mechanisms are separate from the public charge inadmissibility determination and are outside the scope of this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will not require a sponsored immigrant to sue a sponsor for reimbursement as part of the public charge analysis; enforcement arises after admission and interested parties may pursue civil remedies under existing statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud/material concealment grounds for insufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: If DHS finds fraud, material concealment or misrepresentation (including forgery, counterfeiting, falsification of documents) in executing an Affidavit of Support, DHS will determine the Affidavit is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding of such misconduct results in an insufficient affidavit determination and automatic inadmissibility under section 212(a)(4), without further consideration of statutory minimum factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsor relationship not re-evaluated in totality
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a sponsor will actually provide financial support (for example by assessing closeness of relationship) is relevant to assessing the sufficiency of the Affidavit of Support, but DHS will not re-evaluate the sponsor's likelihood of providing support as part of the totality of the circumstances once the affidavit has been found sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS considers such relationship-based inquiries duplicative if already examined during the sufficiency determination and declines to require officers to re-assess them in the public charge analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of HCBS from benefits considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Home- and Community-Based Services (HCBS) will be excluded from consideration in public charge inadmissibility determinations because HCBS do not provide 'total care for basic needs' (they do not pay for room and board) and they promote employment and community participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction, supported by HHS, separates HCBS from long-term institutionalization, which remains a considered category; DHS will not penalize HCBS receipt in public charge analyses.
